explain.say: When you eat, three senses work together. Your tongue tastes, your nose smells, and your mouth feels texture and temperature. Your brain blends them into one flavour.

explain.say: Your tongue has thousands of taste buds, each holding 50 to 150 taste cells. They detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, the savoury taste of things like cheese and tomatoes.

explain.say: The brain combines all three signals with crunch, creaminess and the heat of chilli. The result is the flavour you notice, which is why food tastes so different when one sense is missing.

faq.a: Taste buds are tiny clusters of 50 to 150 taste cells, mostly in the bumps on your tongue. Chemicals dissolved in saliva fit onto receptors on the cells, which then send signals to the brain.
asks: How many taste buds do we have?

faq.q: What are the five basic tastes?
faq.a: The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Umami is the savoury taste found in foods like meat, cheese, mushrooms and tomatoes.
asks: How many tastes can the tongue detect?

faq.q: What is the difference between taste and flavour?
faq.a: Taste is only the five basic tastes from the tongue. Flavour is the whole experience the brain builds from taste, smell, texture and temperature together, and smell supplies most of it.
asks: Is taste the same as flavour?

faq.q: Is there a taste map on the tongue?
faq.a: No. The old idea that sweet is tasted only at the tip and bitter only at the back is a myth. Taste buds all over the tongue can detect all five basic tastes.
asks: Does the tip of the tongue taste sweet?

faq.q: How does smell add to flavour?
faq.a: When you chew and swallow, aroma molecules travel up from the back of your mouth into your nose. Your brain treats these smells as part of the taste, so most of what we call flavour actually comes from smell.
asks: Do we taste with our nose?

facts: A taste bud contains roughly 50 to 150 taste receptor cells.
Taste cells are replaced about every one to two weeks.
The tongue map, with separate zones for each taste, is a myth: all tastes can be detected across the tongue.

quiz.say: Strawberry and raspberry sweets both taste sweet on the tongue. What tells you which is which?
quiz.show: What lets you tell strawberry from raspberry?

quiz.why: Both are sweet to the tongue; their aroma molecules, reaching the nose from the back of the mouth, give each its own flavour.
